Taxpayers' Arkansas Individual Income Tax Returns without first
determining whether the Taxpayers underreported their net taxable
income by 25% or more in the most recent three years (2017, 2018,
and 2019) of the Taxpayers' audit. See Exhibit A. While the Audit

Taxpayers underreported their net taxable income by 25% or more

DFA Tax Auditor erroneously determined that the Taxpayer
were not engaged in for profit under
IRC § 183. See Exhibit C and Exhibit L.
Income Tax Deductions
The Arkansas Income Tax Act of 1929 (as codified under Ark.
Code Ann. § 26-51-101, et seq.) imposes an income tax upon "the
entire income of every [resident and individual]. Ark. Code Ann. §
26-51-201(a) (emphasis added). "The tax shall be levied, collected,
and paid annually upon the entire net income as defined and
computed in this chapter...." Id. "Net income" is derived from
16

adjusting gross income by the deductions allowed by the Arkansas
Income Tax Act of 1929. Id. At § 26-51-403(a).
For purposes of computing net income, the Arkansas Income
Tax Act of 1929 has adopted IRC § 162, which allows a taxpayer
(applicable to individuals and corporations) to deduct all ordinary
and necessary expenses incurred in carrying on a trade or business.
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-423(a)(1). The Arkansas Income Tax Act of
1929 allows a deduction for losses incurred in a trade or business.
Id at § 26-51-424. An expense is "ordinary" if it is "normal, usual, or
customary" in a taxpayer's trade or business. Deputy v. du Pont,
308 U.S. 488, 495 (1940). An expense is "necessary if it is
"appropriate or helpful" for the development of a taxpayer's trade
or business. C.I.R. v. Tellier, 383 U.S. 687, 689 (1966) (citing Welch
v. Helvering, 290 U.S. 111, 113 (1933)). "A 'trade or business,"
although not defined in the tax law, has been characterized as an
activity carried on for a livelihood or for profit." Ark. Admin. Code §
006.05.307-26-51-423(a). Some type of economic activity must be
conducted, and such activity is considered a business if it is entered
into and carried on in good faith for the purpose of making profit.
Id. Whether an expense is deductible under IRC § 162 is a question
of fact to be decided on the basis of all the relevant facts and
circumstances. Cloud v. CI.R.,97 T.C. 613, 618 (1991).
The Arkansas Income Tax Act of 1929 has also adopted IRC §
274, which allows a taxpayer (applicable to individuals and
corporations) to deduct travel expenses. Ark. Code Ann § 26-51-
423(b). Under the IRC, no deduction or credit is allowed under IRC
§ 162 for travel expenses unless the taxpayer substantiates by
adequate records or by sufficient evidence corroborating the
taxpayer's own statement. IRC § 274(d). To deduct travel expenses,
a taxpayer must show that the expense claimed is directly related to
or associated with the active conduct of his or her trade or business.
Heinbockel v. C.I.R., T.C. Memo. 2013-125 at 18; IRC § 274(a). A
taxpayer must also provide adequate records showing the amount
of the expense, the time and place of the expense, and the business
purpose of the expense. Heinbockel, T.C. Memo. 2013-125 at 18.
Tax deductions and credits, like tax exemptions, exist as a
matter of legislative grace. Cook v. Walters Dry Goods Co., 212 Ark.
485, 488, 206 S.W.2d 742, 744 (1947); Kansas City Southern Ry. Co. v.
Pledger, 301 Ark. 564, 567, 785 S.W.2d 462, 464 (1990); Weiss v.
American Honda Finance Corp., 360 Ark. 208, 213, 200 S.W.3d 381, 384
(2004). A taxpayer claiming a deduction or credit bears the burden of
proving that he or she is entitled to the deduction or credit by bringing
himself or herself clearly within the terms and conditions imposed by the
statute that contains the deduction or credit. Weiss, 360 Ark. at 213, 200
S.W.3d at 384.

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
Standard of Proof
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-313(c) (Repl. 2020) provides, in pertinent part, as
follows:
The burden of proof applied to matters of fact and evidence,
whether placed on the taxpayer or the state in controversies
regarding the application of a state tax law shall be by
preponderance of the evidence.
A preponderance of the evidence means the greater weight of the evidence.
Chandler v. Baker, 16 Ark. App. 253, 700 S.W.2d 378 (1985). In Edmisten v. Bull
Shoals Landing, 2014 Ark. 89, at 12-13, 432 S.W.3d 25, 33, the Arkansas Supreme
Court explained:
A preponderance of the evidence is “not necessarily established by the
greater number of witnesses testifying to a fact but by evidence that has
the most convincing force; superior evidentiary weight that, though not
sufficient to free the mind wholly from all reasonable doubt, is still
sufficient to incline a fair and impartial mind to one side of the issue
rather than the other.
The Department bears the burden of proving that the tax law applies to an
item or service sought to be taxed, and a taxpayer bears the burden of proving
entitlement to a tax exemption, deduction, or credit. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-
313(d) (Repl. 2020). Statutes imposing a tax or providing a tax exemption,

their application, giving the words their plain and ordinary meaning. Ark. Code

with respect to the application of a statute imposing a tax or providing a tax
exemption, deduction, or credit, the doubt must be resolved against the
application of the tax, exemption, deduction, or credit. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-

The State of Arkansas imposes an income tax upon “the entire income of
every resident, individual, trust, or estate. The tax shall be levied, collected, and
paid annually upon the entire net income as defined and computed in this
chapter at the following rates . . ..” See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-201(a) (Repl.

deductions. See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-403 (Repl. 2020).

legislative grace. See Cook, Commissioner of Revenue v. Walters Dry Good

or credit by bringing herself or himself clearly within the terms and conditions
imposed by the statute that contains the deduction or credit. See Weiss v.
American Honda Finance Corp., 360 Ark. 208, 200 S.W.3d 381 (2004).
